module_title: Adaptation Mechanisms, ZPD & Kohlberg's Specific Stages
introduction: This intermediate tier drives into the exact mechanical processes of learning. It uncovers Piaget's cognitive schemas, Vygotsky's scaffolding matrix, and breaks down Kohlberg's 3 levels into their 6 specific stages, which are frequent targets in CTET/DSSSB exams.

core_concepts.title: Piaget's Cognitive Processes (Adaptation)
core_concepts.description:
Learning occurs through the continuous modification of **Schemas** (mental frameworks or building blocks of knowledge).
1. Assimilation: Fitting new information into an existing schema without changing it. (e.g., A child knows a dog has 4 legs, sees a cat, and calls it a 'dog').
2. Accommodation: Modifying an existing schema or creating a new one to fit new information. (e.g., The child realizes the cat says 'meow' and creates a new 'cat' schema).
3. Equilibration/Disequilibrium: The biological drive to balance assimilation and accommodation. When new information doesn't fit, it creates cognitive conflict (Disequilibrium), forcing the child to accommodate and reach a new state of understanding (Equilibration).

core_concepts.title: Vygotsky: ZPD and Scaffolding
core_concepts.description:
1. Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD): The critical learning gap. It is the difference between what a learner can do independently (actual developmental level) and what they can do with guidance (potential developmental level).
2. More Knowledgeable Other (MKO): Anyone who has a better understanding of the concept than the learner (teacher, peer, or technology).
3. Scaffolding: Temporary, tailored support provided by an MKO to help the learner cross the ZPD. Examples include cues, prompts, and half-solved problems. As the learner becomes competent, scaffolding is gradually removed (fading).

core_concepts.title: Kohlberg's 6 Stages of Moral Development
core_concepts.description:
Level 1: Pre-Conventional
- Stage 1: Punishment & Obedience Orientation (I won't steal because I will go to jail).
- Stage 2: Instrumental Relativist / Mutual Exchange (Tit-for-tat. I'll help you if you help me).
Level 2: Conventional
- Stage 3: Good Boy / Nice Girl Orientation (I won't steal because my family will think I'm a bad person).
- Stage 4: Law & Order Orientation (I won't steal because the law says stealing is illegal, and rules must be obeyed to prevent chaos).
Level 3: Post-Conventional
- Stage 5: Social Contract (Rules are agreements for the greater good, but can be changed if they fail to serve humanity).
- Stage 6: Universal Ethical Principles (Based on internal conscience, justice, and human life, even if it means breaking the law and facing severe personal consequences).

important_entities.name: Heinz Dilemma
important_entities.key_fact: The tool used by Kohlberg to assess moral stages.
important_entities.significance: A man (Heinz) steals an overpriced drug to save his dying wife. Kohlberg did not care whether a subject said 'Yes, he should steal' or 'No, he shouldn't'. He exclusively analyzed the **REASONING** behind the answer to determine the subject's moral stage.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Scaffolding is strictly **TEMPORARY**. If a teacher continues to solve the math problem for the student every day, it is NOT scaffolding. True scaffolding requires 'fading'—stepping back and transferring responsibility to the child once they show competence.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: **A**ssimilation is **A**dding a paper to an existing file folder. **A**ccommodation is **A**ltering the folder or buying a brand new one.

exam_strategy_tips: If a question says: 'Raman shares his lunch with Sita today because she shared hers with him yesterday', identify this as a classic 'Tit-for-tat' scenario. It directly maps to Kohlberg's **Stage 2: Instrumental Relativist / Mutual Exchange**.
